A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same B-VLLM framework and contain readable text, equations, figures and tables. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes supplementary Sections 7–9. All supplied pages support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original video and image benchmark results, component ablations and token/frame sensitivity experiments in Tables 1–3 and Figure 3.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds architecture comparisons, sensitivity analyses, computational measurements and qualitative evaluations, including supplementary results.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 adds an explicit step restoring selected frames' temporal order using the selection matrix. The frame-selection, temporal-merging, spatial-sampling and optional spatial-merging components otherwise remain unchanged. The supplementary temporal-order limitation is not reconciled with this added step.

E1.justification: The main training datasets and scored video/image benchmark suites are retained. Supplementary Figures 7–10 add qualitative evaluation of an AI-generated video and multi-turn video conversations, extending the demonstrated input and interaction scenarios. Next-QA appears only in Table 6's dataset summary; no corresponding results establish its evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes VideoChatGPT, adds Sharegpt4Video, and adds VideoChat2 participation on VNBench and VideoMME. Supplementary Table 9 introduces comparisons with InternVideo2, InternVL2, LLaVA-OV and Qwen2VL; Table 10 compares latency with Qwen2VL. Tables 4 and 7 also introduce alternative selection architectures and frame features.

E3.justification: Section 3.2 changes the stated temperature from 0.5 to 0.1. Figure 3 replaces the earlier 4–16-frame sweep with 2–32-frame/token sweeps and explicitly evaluates VideoMME-Medium, adding controlled temperature, similarity-threshold and token-budget experiments. New protocols include eight-frame VideoLLaMA2 feature probes and latency measurements for 4-, 8- and 12-minute videos. The original two-stage training recipe is retained in supplementary Section 7.1.

E4.justification: The component ablation in Table 3 is retained, but Figure 3 substantially revises the sensitivity analysis and removes the earlier image-token-count sweep. Added analyses test temperature, merging threshold, token budget, Q-Former versus Resampler, alternative frame features including OCR/counting performance, and frame-count sensitivity across video durations. Supplementary Figures 6–10 add qualitative case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Reported B-VLLM scores change substantially: Table 1 gives MVBench 49.2 to 50.8, VNBench 13.8 to 22.6 and VideoMME-Long 44.4 to 47.9. Changes are mixed: Table 2 gives MME 1504 to 1455 and VizWiz 46.5 to 45.1. Numerous additional comparison, sensitivity and efficiency results appear. These are revised reported outcomes, not established same-setting gains, given the method and setting revisions.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5, the Gumbel-Softmax reasoning, cosine-threshold duplicate definition and averaging rules are retained. Neither version supplies additional theorems, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: v2 specifies a 10% MVBench gain in the abstract/introduction, whereas v1's introduction describes up to 10% improvement to backbone VLLMs more generally. The conclusion replaces its explicit SOTA assertion with effectiveness and limitations, although SOTA language remains elsewhere. The four central contributions are retained.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the earlier eight-frame/eight-token optimum discussion with interpretations of frame-count saturation and a 512-token performance plateau. It adds explanations of temperature and merging effects, Q-Former versus Resampler behavior, and the accuracy–efficiency tradeoff of CLS features. New qualifications address fixed frame-count limits and stronger models' larger training datasets; the earlier multi-round and temporal-order caveats largely move to the supplement.

D1.justification: Supplementary Tables 5–6 and Section 7 add training-data composition, source attribution, benchmark statistics and setup details, including EVA-CLIP, 768 preliminary tokens and 32 selected frames with 32 spatial tokens each. Model sizes and computational costs are also newly reported. The existing training recipe is relocated, not newly introduced; some details are lost, including v1's open-ended grading description and explicit activation-free projection specification.

R1.justification: v2 adds CLS-token literature, training-source references and citations concerning other vision applications, while removing the RegNet reference. The supplement adds brief positioning against newer, larger-data VLLMs. The principal related-work taxonomy and iterative-token-merging novelty assertion remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and selected introductory and discussion passages are edited. Implementation is condensed, training details move to the supplement, and limitations are redistributed between Section 5.4 and supplementary Section 8.6. Despite these organizational refinements, the main section sequence, method exposition and much of the benchmark narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is substantially redesigned with additional heatmaps and a token-budget curve. Figure 4 gains explicit frame-selection timelines, while supplementary Figure 5 and Figures 6–10 add sensitivity and conversation displays. Tables 4–10 are new; existing tables also change caption placement, styling and placement within the document.

improvement.justification: v1 offered limited evidence for its specific selection mechanisms and accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. v2 substantially strengthens their assessment through controlled alternatives in Tables 4 and 7, expanded sensitivity experiments, computational comparisons and previously unavailable dataset/setup details. Newer-baseline comparisons and explicit CLS/frame-count limitations also improve perspective. Latency protocols remain underspecified and some text–table and temporal-order inconsistencies persist, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in methodological scrutiny and reproducibility.
